newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel rights group blasts "routine" abuse of Arabs.
newsitem.headline: Israel rights group blasts "routine" abuse of Arabs.

text.p: A leading Israeli human rights group issued a scathing indictment on Wednesday of systematic Israeli violence towards Palestinians.

B'Tselem levelled its attack against the backdrop of recent police beatings of Arabs, a symbolic fine imposed on soldiers who violated "open-fire" orders in killing a Palestinian and High Court rulings allowing the use of force in interrogations.

"It's very telling of Israeli society that these incidents all happened in the same week. They are phenomena of the same process of the dehumanisation of Palestinians in Israeli society," B'Tselem deputy director Eytan Felner told Reuters.
In an incident broadcast worldwide this week, an amateur cameraman filmed two Israeli policemen beating and abusing Palestinians caught in Jerusalem without work permits.

In the courtyard of an apartment complex, the two policemen kicked some of the Palestinians in the head, kneed another in the stomach and made others do push-ups on the ground. One smiled widely while pretending to ride an Arab like a donkey.
"The beatings are unique only in that a photographer was present at the scene and filmed the incident," B'Tselem said.
The group in September published a report of 10 such instances in June and July. B'Tselem said many more incidents undoubtedly escape the attention of human rights groups.

B'Tselem blasted a military court decision this week which imposed a symbolic fine of one agora (a hundredth of a shekel and worth one third of a U.S. cent) on four Israeli soldiers who shot dead a Palestinian at a West Bank roadblock in 1993.
The court found the men, members of an undercover army unit who were accused of negligently causing the death of Iyad Amali, had violated military "open fire" procedures in the incident.
In imposing the one agora fine, the court rejected a plea bargain proposed by military prosecutors and defence which would have provided for a conditional 30-day sentence, B'Tselem said.
The army has said it would appeal for a tougher punishment, but B'Tselem said it had little faith judges would impose a sentence stiffer than the plea bargain agreed by prosecutors.

Israel's High Court ruled in separate cases last week that Shin Bet secret police could use "physical pressure" against Arabs suspected of belonging to militant Islamic groups to extract information police said could prevent suicide attacks.

One of the rulings, in which the court overturned an interim order barring police from using force, drew the attention of the United Nations Committee against Torture. A U.N. source described the court decision as "institutionalising torture".
A 1987 Israeli commission ruled the Shin Bet could use "moderate physical pressure" in interrogations and "increased physical pressure" when an attack was imminent.
Justices have ruled the Shin Bet can use such methods as violent shaking, prolonged sleep deprivation and forcing detainees to remain in uncomfortable positions for long periods.
"These are not exceptional cases but demonstrate a systematic, routinised system and bureaucracy of violence which results from 30 years of occupation of the Palestinians," Felner said.
The government did not immediately repsond to B'Tselem's accusations but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did comment on the High Court's approval of limited use of force on suspects.

"We are a democratic country respectful of human rights that is threatened by wild people who have no respect for human rights who blow up buses, who blow up airplanes," he told U.S. television network CNN.
"The question of what are the rights of the innocent as against the rights of jailed terrorists is a very difficult one that I wouldn't have any solution to."
